newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says no plan to introduce index warrants.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says no plan to introduce index warrants.

text.p: Taiwan's securities watchdog said on Thursday it had no plans to introduce warrants linked to the Taiwan Stock Exchange's weighted index, but would launch warrant issues based on more than 20 Taiwan firms in June.
"We have no plans to introduce warrants linked to the Taiwan stock index," Lee Chi-hsien, a deputy director of the Securities and Exchange Commission, told Reuters by telephone.
"But since the index is our proprietary product, we have the right to decide whether to let anyone else use it or not," Lee said. The commission is the supervisor of the Taiwan exchange.

Lee's comments followed a statement by the Taiwan Stock Exchange on Wednesday in which it expressed "serious concern and objection" regarding plans by two foreign institutions to set up derivative warrants linked to the Taiwan index.

Hong Kong's Peregrine Derivatives Limited and Union Bank of Switzerland on Wednesday listed their issued call warrants, linked to the Taiwan Stock Exchange's weighted index, on the Hong Kong exchange, the statement said.

"Because these companies have not been authorised by the Taiwan Stock Exchange to use its index, the exchange has issued an urgent letter to the two firms to express serious concern and objection and reserve the rights for necessary legal actions," the Taiwan Stock Exchange said.
The commission's Lee said Taiwan would not allow outsiders to use the index because such an access would cause the market to become volatile.
"Even if we don't use it, we will not necessarily let others use it because such warrant issue might affect our market," he said.
He denied a Hong Kong newspaper report that the commission prohibited Hong Kong firms from issuing warrants linked to the Taiwan index because it wanted to be the first to introduce the products.
Lee said the commission would seek legal recourse if other foreign institutions began issuing warrants based on the Taiwan index.
"I don't know why these foreign firms think they are entitled to do this," he said. "Simply ask them to use Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index to issue warrants. Will the Hong Kong exchange agree?"
Taiwan's Foreign Minister Paul Chiu had said earlier in April that the island would allow local and foreign institutions to issue warrants on Taiwan stocks by the end of June.
But Lee said the stock index still would not be open to warrant trading.
Local and foreign banks and securities brokerages needed to have a minimum capital of T$3 billion to issue warrants on locally listed firms, Chiu said in early April.

Under the proposal, warrant issues would be limited to listed shares that posted a market value of more than T$30 billion (US$1.1 billion) and had 25 percent or more of their shares circulating in the market.
The listed companies also must have more than 7,500 shareholders.

More than 20 local listed companies -- including Cathay Life, Chang Hwa Bank, First Commercial Bank, Hua Nan Bank, Nan Ya Plastics, Formosa Plastics and China Steel -- qualify under the proposed guidelines.
